item.title: American Nero: Why Trump is trying to burn down the National Academy of Sciences
item.description:
By Benjamin Santer | Opinion | July 26, 2026

In a post on Truth Social earlier this month, Trump claimed that the National Academy of Sciences published “fraudulent, biased, and misleading Manuals on climate change.” He has now ordered “Federal Suspension and Debarment Officials” to review the organization’s conduct.

Although he referred to multiple “Manuals,” the president’s Truth Social screed is really about a single manual: the Federal Judicial Center’s Reference Manual on Scientific Evidence. The Reference Manual serves “as a go-to document judges can use when they deal with issues involving scientific testimony.” For the first time, the most recent version of the manual  contains a climate science chapter. It describes the hard scientific evidence that fossil fuel burning is influencing extreme weather events. This science is anathema to the oil industry and to its conservative supporters, including the president, and they have responded by attacking the manual and its authors.

The Federal Judicial Center caved to a request by 27 Republican state attorneys general to remove the climate chapter from the Reference Manual, but it is still publicly available on the website of the National Academy of Sciences. This open defiance of overt political pressure is causing problems for the National Academies.

Established by President Abraham Lincoln in 1863, the National Academy of Sciences is the premier scientific organization in the United States. One part of its mission is to produce and promote “the adoption of independent, authoritative, trusted scientific advice to the government for the benefit of society.”

I’m a member of the National Academy of Sciences. I’m also a climate scientist. I’m writing this essay as a private citizen, not as a representative of the official or unofficial views of the academy. I simply care about its survival.

I’ve written and spoken about Trump’s views on climate science since 2014. In essays, op-eds, podcasts, and open letters—including an open letter to Trump himself. It’s painful and disheartening to recognize that nothing I’ve written has made one iota of difference. Trump continues to incorrectly dismiss climate science as a fraud. As a con job. As a hoax.

The real fraud is Donald J. Trump. The real hoax is in Trump’s efforts to persuade Americans that human-caused climate change is not happening. That wildfires are solely due to bad forest management. Or to Canadians. The real con job is in Trump’s repeated lies about global warming. That it isn’t happening. That all changes in climate are purely natural.

Trump is destroying so much that is good and valuable in America. He’s generating the very “American carnage” he described in his first inauguration speech. Carnage in pursuit of power, revenge, personal financial gain, and ego. He is remaking the country in his own image.

Now the National Academy of Sciences is firmly in his sights.

Why? Why does he care about an organization of scientists? A confederacy of nerds? Why does he care about climate science? Why does he believe, falsely, that climate science is fraudulent?

The National Academy of Sciences is on Trump’s radar because they are in his way. The climate science the National Academy of Sciences has assessed, for over four decades, is in fundamental conflict with Trump’s political agenda: the promotion of fossil fuels and the promotion of the powerful fossil fuel interests that have supported Trump’s rise. Science shows that fossil fuel burning is affecting Earth’s climate in harmful ways. So in Trump world, science is the enemy.

The cause of President Trump’s attack on the National Academy of Sciences is simple. The National Academy of Sciences is good at what it does. It has published reports on pretty much every aspect of climate science, most recently on what’s called “event attribution,” or the influence of human-caused climate change on extreme events.

Event attribution research provides hard evidence that fossil-fueled warming is ratcheting up the intensity and frequency of heat waves, and of extreme rainfall. This is the kind of evidence that may put fossil fuel companies on the hook for damages in lawsuits. As the tobacco industry learned decades ago, knowingly causing harm to human health can affect your corporate bottom line. The fossil fuel companies will eventually learn the same lesson.

But not under Donald Trump’s watch. He will do all he can to shield the Exxons and Chevrons of the world from accountability. If shielding means destroying the National Academy of Sciences, then so be it. If shielding means crippling the ability of this country’s leading institutions to monitor global warming, to study it with sophisticated computer models, and to understand the causes of warming, then so be it. If shielding means actively discouraging the use of cheap, efficient sources of low carbon energy, then so be it. If shielding means coming up with deeply flawed government reports that portray climate science as unsettled, then so be it.

President Trump doesn’t like bad news. Human-caused global warming is bad news. It’s bad news for his deep-pocketed supporters in the fossil fuel industry. It’s bad news for the narrative that under Trump’s tenure, everything is wonderful in America. It’s bad news for the fiction that the country’s future is bright.

But our future is not bright. It’s hot. It’s a future with lots of bad news and “downers.” Excess mortality from increasingly more intense heat waves is a downer. Larger, more intense wildfires are a downer, burning not only our forests, but also our cities, and leaving us choking in acrid smoke. Sea-level rise is a downer, taking billions of dollars off the value of coastal real estate.

This is why Trump is so exercised about the National Academy of Sciences. He doesn’t want event attribution reports. He doesn’t want fast-track reports assessing the evidence for human effects on global climate. He doesn’t want US courts to have a climate science chapter in the Reference Manual on Scientific Evidence, which provides judges with credible, vetted information about the reality, seriousness, costs, and causes of climate change.

It’s said that Nero fiddled while Rome burned. Others have argued he actually started the fire, so that he could rebuild the city to his liking. We cannot allow our American Nero to fuel the flames while the planet burns with his reckless pro-fossil fuel policies. And we cannot allow him to destroy institutions—like the US National Academies of Science, Engineering, and Medicine—that provide a candle in the growing darkness of ignorance.


The Bulletin elevates expert voices above the noise. But as an independent nonprofit organization, our operations depend on the support of readers like you. Help us continue to deliver quality journalism that holds leaders accountable. Your support of our work at any level is important. In return, we promise our coverage will be understandable, influential, vigilant, solution-oriented, and fair-minded. Together we can make a difference.

Keywords: Donald Trump, National Academy of Sciences, attacks on science, climate crisis, fossil fuel industry
Topics: Climate Change, Opinion

item.title: Southern China faces torrential rain, flood risk after Typhoon Noul hits land
item.description:
Typhoon Noul will dump heavy to torrential rains across much of southern China for two days, authorities said, after sweeping the province of Guangdong and neighboring Hong Kong with gale-force winds, following landfall on Sunday.

China declared its highest alert for flash floods in several provinces as the year's strongest typhoon forced the relocation of more than 700,000 people in Guangdong, authorities said.

The year's 12th tropical cyclone and China's third this month, Noul, which means the glow of sunrise or sunset in Korean, struck the coast of Huidong county at about 3:50 a.m., provincial officials said.

It is expected to bring strong winds and heavy rain to nearby provinces such as Jiangxi and Hunan as it moves inland, state broadcaster CCTV said, with the rains likely to persist until Tuesday.

Extremely heavy to exceptional downpours are expected to lash some areas including the province of Fujian, as the National Meteorological Center forecast heavy to torrential rain from Sunday until Monday morning across much of China's south.

Typhoon weakening as it moves inland

Authorities urged local governments to pay special attention to flood-prone areas such as mountainous and riverine zones, building sites, valleys, and bridges.

The typhoon is weakening as it moves inland, Hong Kong's Observatory said, though southwesterly gales pounded parts of the Asian financial hub, where authorities downgraded the typhoon signal to No. 3 from No. 8 by afternoon.

Overnight, the storm had passed within 80 km of Hong Kong.

Hong Kong airport authorities said flights will gradually resume on Sunday afternoon, after being mostly suspended for more than 12 hours.

item.title: Trump Blames Canada For Smoke From A Climate America Created - CleanTechnica
item.description:
Trump Blames Canada For Smoke From A Climate America Created

Support CleanTechnica's work through

a Substack subscription,

on Patreon, or

on Stripe. Help us produce all of the

high-quality, original content we publish week after weekdespite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

Donald Trump says Canada is poisoning American cities with wildfire smoke. He has told Prime Minister Mark Carney to get the fires under control, demanded compensation and threatened tariffs because smoke from Canadian fires crossed into the United States. The smoke did come from trees burning in Canada. That establishes the immediate source of the pollution, but says very little about the larger causes of the conditions producing fires of this scale.

The border tells us where the forests caught fire. It does not allocate responsibility for the hotter and drier conditions that have made North American wildfire seasons longer, larger and harder to control. Trump is treating the location of the burning trees as though it settles the climate question. It does not.

From 1850 through 2024, the United States produced about 24% of cumulative global fossil CO₂ emissions. The current EU27 produced about 16%, China 15% and India 4%. The United States has held the largest cumulative national total since 1917. A separate peer-reviewed assessment of national contributions to warming from historical CO₂, methane and nitrous oxide also puts the United States first.

China now emits more CO₂ annually, a comparison frequently used to divert attention from the cumulative nature of carbon dioxide. The climate influencing current wildfire conditions was not created by emissions from the latest reporting year. It was built over generations. The United States industrialized early, consumed fossil fuels on an exceptional scale, organized transport and land use around oil, and received enormous economic benefits from doing so. No individual country contributed more to the accumulated warming now affecting forests across the continent.

The fires are in Canada. The climate conditions affecting them are not exclusively Canadian, and the United States has contributed more to those conditions than any other country.

Climate attribution science does not claim that carbon dioxide starts individual fires. It examines how warming changes the conditions in which fires start and spread. Higher temperatures dry vegetation and soils, intensify drought, lengthen fire seasons and increase the probability that fires will grow beyond the capacity of suppression systems. Climate change does not have to increase the number of ignitions dramatically to produce much greater damage. It can do so by increasing the area capable of sustaining large fires and extending the period during which they can burn.

The peer-reviewed attribution analysis of Canada’s catastrophic 2023 fire season found that human-caused climate change more than doubled the likelihood of an area burned that large in eastern and southwestern Canada. It made an exceptionally long fire season more than five times as likely and increased the likelihood of simultaneous extreme fire weather across widely separated regions. Canada did not experience a record number of ignitions. The exceptional outcome came from fires becoming unusually large, persistent and geographically widespread.

There is not yet an event-attribution study assigning a precise climate fraction to the fires burning this week. That means a precise fraction should not be invented. It does not mean the established relationship between warming and severe Canadian wildfire conditions should be ignored until a paper addressing this exact event is published. Scientific caution about a particular percentage is not evidence that the broader causal relationship is uncertain.

Trump’s compensation demand therefore reverses the more important responsibility. The United States is not merely an uninvolved neighbour receiving pollution produced entirely by another country’s choices. It is the largest historical national contributor to the warming that has increased the likelihood and severity of this class of disaster.

Under any serious system of transboundary climate accountability, the United States would face far larger claims arising from its historical emissions than it could plausibly make against Canada for wildfire smoke.

The American responsibility is not confined to emissions released by people who died generations ago. The United States continues to make political choices that protect fossil fuel production and weaken climate policy. In 2016, the Electoral College installed Trump despite his losing the popular vote. In 2024, Americans returned him to office with 312 electoral votes and 49.8% of the national popular vote after having already seen his approach to climate science, environmental regulation and fossil fuel development.

There was little room for misunderstanding the second time. Americans had watched repeated megafires, smoke emergencies, heat waves, floods and billion-dollar disasters. They had seen Trump withdraw the United States from the Paris Agreement during his first term. They knew he opposed greenhouse gas regulation, promoted expanded fossil extraction and treated climate policy as an obstacle to economic growth.

Many voters ranked immigration, inflation, cultural grievance, partisan loyalty or gasoline prices above climate stability. That is their democratic right. It does not remove responsibility for the foreseeable climate consequences of the government they selected. Elections produce governments with entire policy programs, not individually chosen menu items. A voter may not have supported Trump because of his climate policies, but those policies were neither concealed nor incidental.

Enough Americans approved of them, accepted them or considered them unimportant enough to overlook that Trump returned to power. Since then, his administration has again withdrawn the United States from the Paris Agreement. His EPA has rescinded the 2009 greenhouse gas Endangerment Finding and repealed federal greenhouse gas standards for light-, medium- and heavy-duty vehicles. The federal government is weakening measures intended to reduce future climate risk while blaming Canada for failing to contain one of its consequences.

This does not make every American equally responsible. Children with asthma did not vote for the administration. Millions of Americans voted against it. Noncitizens could not vote, and lower-income households with poor access to filtration will often suffer more than wealthier people with greater political influence and better protection from smoke.

Those inequities matter, but they do not eliminate collective political responsibility. Governments act in the name of countries, national emissions accumulate regardless of internal political disagreement, and elections determine which policies will be pursued. Americans who opposed Trump’s climate agenda can accurately say they fought against it. The United States as a political community cannot claim that the choice was never made.

Canada deserves no general climate absolution. It is a wealthy, high-emitting fossil fuel producer whose governments have protected oil and gas production while repeatedly missing climate targets. Canadian emissions in 2024 were still 685 MtCO₂e, only 10.3% below 2005 and 12.6% above 1990. Oil and gas emissions were 5.1% higher than in 2005, while Canada’s own projections show current policies falling well short of its 2030 commitment.

Canada also has direct responsibility for protecting communities, improving evacuation systems, funding firefighting capacity, using Indigenous-led cultural fire where appropriate and managing fuels around settlements. Some losses will reflect inadequate preparation, poor land management or delayed responses by Canadian governments.

Those failures do not make the two countries equally responsible for climate change, and they do not turn the United States into an innocent downwind victim. Canada’s smaller population does not excuse its high per-capita emissions or fossil fuel expansion. Equally, Canada’s failures do not erase the much greater absolute historical contribution of the United States.

Nor can Canada extinguish every fire across the boreal forest simply because smoke is moving toward American cities. Canada contains millions of square kilometres of forest, much of it remote and sparsely populated. Lightning storms can create many simultaneous fires, including fires that become very large before crews can reach them. Attempting to suppress every remote fire would be physically impossible, ecologically damaging and extraordinarily expensive. The relevant questions concern preparation, priorities and protection of communities, not the fantasy that a national government can prevent a continental forest system from burning.

Trump’s argument depends on treating the border as decisive when smoke moves south and irrelevant when greenhouse gases move north. The atmosphere recognizes neither distinction. American emissions spread globally, contributed substantially to continental warming and helped intensify the conditions in which Canadian forests now burn. Canadian smoke is returning through that same shared atmosphere.

The United States is breathing smoke from Canadian fires. It is also experiencing a climate risk that it did more than any other country to create and that its voters have again chosen not to treat as a governing priority. Blaming Canada may be politically convenient, but it does not survive contact with the emissions record, attribution science or the policies Americans knowingly put back into office.

Previously published on TFIE Strategy Briefing.

item.title: Military bosses say climate change is now a national security threat – ministers must not ignore them
item.description:
Military bosses say climate change is now a national security threat – ministers must not ignore them

A leaked military report has warned that prolonged high temperatures and volatility in weather patterns now pose an existential risk to Britain's food security, economy and geopolitical stability. If the government is unwilling to heed that warning, Britain will become less secure, says Lord Deben

For the first time ever, the British military has warned the government that climate change and the damage we have done to nature seriously threaten our national security.

These are not tree-hugging environmental campaigners, but top-level, hard-bitten military men carrying out their official duty of telling the truth to power.

Their report so frightened government ministers, and showed them to be so unprepared, that they banned its publication. Instead, the public was only allowed a pared-down version, with all the stark reality removed.

That tactic also suited the opposition. Normally, the Tories would be carrying out a relentless campaign to get the full truth. However, that would undermine their current downplaying of climate disruption, so they have been largely silent.

It’s only through leaks that we electors have learned the truth. The men and women we rely on to defend us believe that our homeland is under real threat. They say that we may well not be able to feed our people; that our GDP could be hit twice as hard as it was in the financial crisis; and that a Himalayan water shortage could trigger nuclear engagement between China, Pakistan and India. They also point to the increasing pressure of migrants moving across the world as their own countries become too hot to be habitable or to produce the food they need. They even warn that the warming of the permafrost could release dangerous pathogens, including anthrax.

Now, this isn’t the military seeking more resources for themselves. It is a clear statement that, unless we take action on protecting nature, conserving water, increasing home food production and countering climate change, our homeland is not safe, nor can it be defended.

Ministers have sought to dismiss the military fears as “worst-case scenarios“, and they talk up their increased spending on flood prevention and regenerative agriculture. Yet we have to act to prevent the worst-case scenario if we are to reduce the threat to a level with which we can cope. It is climate change that sets the timetable for that action. Pretending we have the time to move at a more gentle pace is just wishful thinking. We need the force of this military assessment to jerk us back into reality.

And that assessment centres on the likelihood that we will not be able to feed our people. Today, as we look out over the parched fields of England and prepare for yet another heatwave, the scale of the problem is all too evident. It took just three days of unaccustomed heat to cut UK milk production by 11 per cent. Last week, water shortages halted Britain’s biggest chicken-processing factory, which could only get started again by trucking in water by road. With no rain for more than a month, farmers warn of significantly reduced yields and widespread shortages of feed for livestock. In Britain’s breadbasket, the East of England, the wheat harvest may well be halved.

All this cannot be dismissed as one bad year. Climate risk has become a present reality. This is now the British climate – torrential downpours in winter and heatwaves in summer. We are almost entirely unprepared for this change. Indeed, funding to enable farmers to adapt has been slashed by both the government and the private sector. The independent experts – the Climate Change Committee – have warned that, at this rate, the UK’s high-quality productive land area will fall from 40 per cent to just over 10 per cent by 2050 because we are simply not making the investment necessary to cope with our changed climate.

And there’s nowhere else in the world from which we can make up the deficit in food production. What’s happening here is happening everywhere – indeed, we are more fortunate than most. Wildfires from Spain to Canada and China are destroying crops on a vast scale. Goldman Sachs says that, over the next two years, food shortages will push prices up by 16 per cent. It is likely that rice yields will fall by about 20 per cent, hit by the heat and water shortage.

Prolonged high temperatures will mean that whole areas of Africa, Asia and South America will become unproductive, and their peoples will have to look elsewhere for food. Britain, which now has to import nearly half of its food, will be particularly exposed, and that fundamentally undermines our national security.

The military rightly emphasise that we need soldiers, ships and drones if we are to defend ourselves. But they also make clear that, if we cannot feed our people, those defences will be to no avail.

Yet, unlike so many others, Britain can turn this around. We have the water we need and, if we invest now, we can get it to the places where it is needed. Properly supported, with access to advanced technology, our farmers can become much more productive. If we refuse to listen to the voices of complacency and fix our sights on stopping runaway climate change by 2050, we can make our nation more secure and help the world to avoid catastrophe.

Lord Deben was chairman of the Climate Change Committee

item.title: Mapping Inherited Infrastructure Risk to account for Power and ICT Dependencies in ...
item.description: Mapping Inherited Infrastructure Risk to account for Power and ICT Dependencies in Climate Risk and Vulnerability Assessments of Smart Road Networks Understanding interdependencies between infrastructure systems is the most urgent infrastructure risk in the forthcoming Technical Report for the UK Climate Change Risk Assessment. This project investigates interdependency cascades within the West Midlands Combined Authority area, providing an in-depth understanding of the systemic risks between road, power and Information and Communications Technology (ICT) networks. The approach currently accounts for power outages which cause total signal inundation and will be further applied to ICT failures which disrupt adaptive optimisation. This pinpoints signals at risk to losing their functional and/or optimisation abilities, capturing the layered functionality inherent in modern urban infrastructure. A GIS-based methodology is presented to assess the upstream risks related to traffic signals, being the critical interface for road operability, using connectivity data to map dependency chains inclusive of physical cables. Through adopting principles from mapping Climate Risk and Vulnerability Assessments (CRVAs), risk scores for power and ICT assets are calculated using the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s conceptual risk framework. Heat, cold, pluvial flooding, fluvial flooding and wind hazard maps are combined with direct vulnerability, criticality and exposure scores. Inherited risk scores for downstream assets can then calculated, through the accumulation of risk scores across dependency chains, from upstream to downstream, indicating the likelihood of power and/or ICT outages throughout the road network. Preliminary results visualise the inherited risk to road operability from ‘high risk’ to ‘low risk’ at 100m x 100m resolution, based on systemic power risks, with additional maps indicating the inherited risk to electricity distribution service areas. Future work will implement the integration of ICT dependencies, where traffic signal states can then be categorised by likely disruption type for adaptation planning and implementation. This research bridges the gap between interdependency cascade modelling and CRVAs, enhancing urban resilience, policy relevance and practical applicability. Speaker/s Harry Kirby

item.title: Attributing Climate Hazards at UNESCO World Heritage Sites | Royal Meteorological Society
item.description: Attributing Climate Hazards at UNESCO World Heritage Sites Climate change poses threats to the Outstanding Universal Value of UNESCO World Heritage Sites (WHSs). While the impacts of a warming world are increasingly visible, quantifying the specific human contribution to heritage-specific climate risks remains a challenge. This research presents a broad-scale, index-based attribution assessment of over 1,000 cultural WHSs to bridge the gap between climate attribution science and heritage field.Using the Max Planck Institute Grand Ensemble (MPI-GE) climate simulations, we contrast a factual scenario with a counterfactual scenario for the recent-past period. The study focuses on two sets of indicators: standard meteorological extremes (extreme heat days, heavy rainfall, and consecutive dry days) and heritage-specific deterioration indices (including salt crystallization, frost intensity, and biological decay).Our results reveal a clear anthropogenic signal across the WHSs. Human influence has added an average of 46 days of extreme heat annually, with the most pronounced increases occurring in low-latitude regions. Furthermore, by integrating World Bank income data as a proxy for adaptive capacity, the study demonstrates a ”risk inequality." WHSs in lower-income countries often face a severe burden: they are exposed to higher intensities of anthropogenically intensified hazards while having fewer financial and institutional resources for adaptation.This work provides quantitative evidence for climate change risk assessment in the heritage field. By attributing specific hazard changes to human activities, the findings support informed management strategies and highlight the urgent need for site-specific adaptation that accounts for both climatic risks and socioeconomic vulnerability. Speaker/s Shixin Zhao

item.title: Ford recalls more than 36000 vehicles in Canada over fire risk - CTV News
item.description: Ford Motor Co. is recalling over 36,000 Broncos in Canada after finding issues in the engine compartment wiring harness. On Friday, Ford said that it will be recalling approximately 36,061 Model Year 2021-2026 Ford Bronco vehicles. A company spokesperson stated in an email that the protective wrapping on the engine compartment wiring harness may be “insufficient”. Over time, as the harness rubs against nearby components, the friction could cause short circuits or electric sparks and lead to smoke, melting or an underhood engine compartment fire. The company will authorize and fund pickup and delivery of the affected vehicles. Ford dealers will inspect the vehicles’ wiring harness, wrap it in a heavy-duty protective sleeve and secure with wear-resistant tape to prevent future rubbing, according to the emailed statement. The repairs will be available for service as of next month. Customers will not have to pay for the repairs, the statement added. The company will also authorize rental vehicle coverage so customers can stay mobile while their vehicle is being services. Customers can determine if their vehicle is included in this recall by entering their Vehicle Identification Number (VIN) here. In the U.S., the company is recalling over half a million Broncos in the same model to inspect the vehicles for wiring harness issues. Ford’s number for this recall is 26S55. Drivers in the U.S. can search their vehicles on NHTSA.gov. NHTSA’s number for this recall campaign is 26V468. In June, the car company issued a recall for more than 16,000 Ford Expedition models citing a “safety risk” with the centre console that could cause injury. In a recall posted twice to Transport Canada, the automaker said the chrome plating on the centre console on certain SUV vehicles could “bubble and peel.” That recall affected Ford Expedition models from the years 2018 to 2024, the notice said. With files from The Associated Press

item.title: Column: Oregon's unnecessary climate bill | The Bulletin
item.description:
Column: Oregon’s unnecessary climate bill

Published 6:00 am Sunday, July 26, 2026

My new favorite unnecessary thing accomplished by the Oregon Legislature was passing the Climate Resilience Investment Act in 2025.

It was both unnecessary and good at the same time.

The Climate Resilience Investment Act requires the Oregon Investment Council and the state treasurer to take action to ensure they manage risks from climate change to state investments. The state controls billions of dollars in investments, including the money invested to pay for the state retirement plan, PERS.

“I could make an argument that this bill was not necessary.”

You know who said that?

Oregon State Treasurer Elizabeth Steiner. Steiner was the bill’s champion.

The bill didn’t go that far.

The Climate Resilience Investment Act was not a divestment bill. It didn’t require the state to get its investments out of fossil fuels or away from carbon.

Fundamentally, it didn’t require the state to change its focus from prioritizing risks and rewards when choosing investments. The goal for state investments is still: Get good returns. Investment in oil, gas and coal may no longer be as welcome as they once were. It does not mean the state would never hold such investments. The decision would have to be a sound one financially.

The bill also required an annual report to the Legislature. The report is the bill’s benefit.

The report is supposed to measure the carbon intensity of the state’s investments. The report issued earlier this year does show a decline in Oregon investments in fossil fuels and more toward clean energy.

The report says that: Emissions intensity in the Oregon Public Employees Retirement Fund dropped by more than 50%; climate-positive investments within the Real Assets portfolio increased from $1.2 billion as of January 1, 2022 to $2.4 billion as of June 30, 2025; Although fossil fuel holdings in Private Market funds increased from January 1, 2022, into 2023, that marked the peak for such investments and was the last time there was a year-over-year increase.

Since January 1, 2023 fossil fuel holdings have steadily declined.

Go deeper into the report and there are also warnings: “Many countries are retreating from net zero ambition and are not public with the data.” There are gaps in data and data reporting is not standardized. In other words, it can be difficult to pin down what is going on in some state investments.

The bottom line conclusion, though, is positive for people who want less carbon-intense Oregon investment. That direction is not because of the Climate Resilience Act. It is because of the direction of the market. Fossil fuels are not done and finished. The business case for green energy or companies taking action to avoid climate risk often makes them the smart investments. And that was before the war in Iran disrupted global oil prices.

“This work has not been without controversy,” Steiner wrote in the report. “Some feel we have gone too far, too fast. Others feel we have not gone far enough.”

The bill did not go that far. The market was already going.

Richard Coe is editorial page editor at The Bulletin and can be reached at richard.coe@bendbulletin.com.
